'''''Lathyrus aphaca''''', known as the '''yellow [[pea]]''' or '''yellow [[vetchling]]''', is an annual species in the family [[Fabaceae]] with yellow flowers and solitary, pea-like fruits. It originated in the [[Middle East]] and has spread throughout [[Europe]] and beyond as a weed of cultivated fields and roadsides. The fruits are eaten as a supplement to diets in some parts of [[South Asia]] but are narcotic and potentially toxic in large quantities.

== Description ==
''Lathyrus aphaca'', known as the yellow [[pea]] or yellow [[vetchling]], is an annual species in the family [[Fabaceae]] (formerly Leguminosae). Plants grow to about 100 cm tall, are pale green to glaucous, glabrous, and have angled but unwinged stems. The leaves are reduced to simple (unbranched) tendrils and what look like leaves are actually stipules, which are ovate-hastate in shape and up to 50 mm long. The flowers are usually solitary and yellow (often streaked with violet), 10–13 mm in length, and held on long (up to 50 mm) stalks branching from the leaf axils. The flowers, which are bisexual, have 10 stamens and 1 style. ''Lathyrus aphaca'' is diploid, with 14 chromosomes.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-55337-7}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==

It is believed to have evolved in the [[Middle East]], around [[Syria]] and [[Jordan]], along with other leguminous species which have a centre of diversity in that region.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lie |first1=T.A. |title=Co-evolution of the legume-Rhizobium association |journal=Plant Soil |date=1987 |volume=100 |issue=1–3 |pages=171–181 |doi=10.1007/BF02370940 |bibcode=1987PlSoi.100..171L |s2cid=33048140 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Smýkal |first1=Petr |title=Legume Crops Phylogeny and Genetic Diversity for Science and Breeding |journal=Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences |date=2015 |volume=34 |issue=1–3 |pages=43–104 |doi=10.1080/07352689.2014.897904 |bibcode=2015CRvPS..34...43S |s2cid=84398165 |url=https://research.birmingham.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/legume-crops-phylogeny-and-genetic-diversity-for-science-and-breeding(a8d2c243-59cd-4e6c-ad21-175d55497152).html}}</ref> Edible species of pea were first cultivated in the [[Fertile Crescent]], while weeds such as ''L. aphaca'' are believed to have adapted naturally to an arable or similar human-disturbed habitat between about 23,000 and 11,000 years ago.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Snir |first1=A. |title=The Origin of Cultivation and Proto-Weeds, Long Before Neolithic Farming |journal=PLOS ONE |date=2015 |volume=10 |issue=7 |article-number=e0131422 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0131422 |pmid=26200895 |pmc=4511808 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2015PLoSO..1031422S }}</ref> ''Lathyrus aphaca'' itself has some advantages as a farmland weed, being able to [[Nitrogen fixation|fix nitrogen]] and thus help to fertilise the soil, as well as being edible in small quantities if present in the grain harvest,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dubey |first1=C. |title=Nutritional and antinutritional evaluation of forest and hybrid legume seeds |journal=Electronic Journal of Environmental, Agricultural and Food Chemistry |date=2008 |volume=7 |pages=2900–2905 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228346135}}</ref> although it is [[narcotic]] when consumed in larger amounts.

The native habitat of ''L. aphaca'' is most likely to be the dry, limestone scrubland in the Middle East sometimes known as phrygana or [[garrigue]]. In these countries it is found in both wild and cultivated habitats.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Danin |first1=A. |title=2010 |url=https://flora.org.il |website=Flora of Israel Online |access-date=8 January 2022}}</ref> It can be an aggressive agricultural weed, infesting mainly wheat,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aamir |first1=M. |title=Germination Ecology of Lathyrus aphaca, a Problematic Weed of Wheat Crop under Semi-Arid Conditions of Pakistan |journal=Planta Daninha |date=2019 |volume=37 |article-number=e019185755 |doi=10.1590/S0100-83582019370100048 |s2cid=196685832|doi-access=free }}</ref> but also other crops, such as [[sugarcane]] in [[Pakistan]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Khan |first1=R.U. |title=Weed flora of sugarcane in district Bannu, Khyber Pakhtunkhawa, Pakistan |journal=Pakistan Journal of Weed Science Research |date=2012 |volume=18 |pages=541–552 |url=https://www.cabi.org/ISC/abstract/20133131786 |archive-date=2022-01-08 |access-date=2022-01-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220108190006/https://www.cabi.org/ISC/abstract/20133131786 }}</ref> The expansion of farming over the last 10,000 years allowed ''L. aphaca'' to increase its range to southern Asia, as far as [[Bangladesh]], and southern Europe as far as [[Portugal]] and even the [[Azores]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=RBG Kew |title=Plants of the World Online |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:501579-1 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=8 January 2022}}</ref> In these regions it is often considered native, but it is more likely that it is an ancient introduction, or [[archaeophyte]], which has found a natural or semi-natural analogue of its phrygana habitat, where it can persist in the wild. In Portugal it is considered native only in the Calcareous Western Centre biome,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Anon. |title=Proceedings of the VII Flora Europaea Symposium, Coimbra, 22-31 May, 1972 |date=1973}}</ref> despite being present throughout the country as an agricultural weed. It is more likely that it is a well-established archaeophyte there.

In northern Europe, ''L. aphaca'' has not generally found any semi-natural analogue of its native arid scrub habitat. In [[Poland]] it is described as occurring 'in a different type of habitats, e.g. in the vegetation of forest edges representing the ''Trifolio-Geranietea sanguinei'' class, on dry lawns, transport route edges (especially along railway lines), in orchards, arable fields and fallows.'<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nobis |first1=A. |title=Lathyrus aphaca L.: the distribution, habitats and remarks on the status of the species in Poland |journal=Acta Soc. Bot. Pol. |date=2011 |volume=80 |issue=3 |pages=237–244 |doi=10.5586/asbp.2011.012 |s2cid=56243363|doi-access=free }}</ref>
Since the early 20th century, it has gone into decline throughout Europe due to improved seed cleaning techniques, and it has largely been eradicated from cereal crops. In the [[Netherlands]], it has declined by 75-100% since 1950,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sparrius |first1=L. |title=Rode Lijst Vaatplanten 2012 volgens Nederlandse en IUCN-criteria |url=https://www.nationalredlist.org/rode-lijst-vaatplanten-2012-volgens-nederlandse-en-iucn-criteria-red-list-of-vascular-plants-2012-according-to-dutch-and-iucn-criteria/ |access-date=8 January 2022 |archive-date=8 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220108190007/https://www.nationalredlist.org/rode-lijst-vaatplanten-2012-volgens-nederlandse-en-iucn-criteria-red-list-of-vascular-plants-2012-according-to-dutch-and-iucn-criteria/ }}</ref> and in Germany and Poland there is a similar story. Meanwhile, however, it has become established as an agricultural weed further afield, in the United States, South Africa and Australia.<ref>{{cite web |last1=GBIF |title=Lathyrus aphaca L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/5356649}}</ref>

== In the United Kingdom ==
[[File:Lathyrus aphaca and Vicia villosa sward.jpg| thumb|Sward of ''Lathyrus aphaca'' at Swanscombe]]
In Britain yellow vetchling has been recorded since 1632,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Clarke |first1=W.A. |title=First Records of British Flowering Plants |date=1900 |publisher=West, Newman & Co. |location=London}}</ref> when it was found by Thomas Johnson near Gravesend. This is sufficiently early to earn it a place as either a native or a long-naturalised arable weed ([[archaeophyte]]), as opposed to a recent introduction ([[neophyte (botany)|neophyte]]). In the absence of any further information, therefore, British authors are free to describe it as a native or an introduced plant as they choose. A semi-natural habitat suggests that it is native, whereas an arable field suggests an archaeophyte. Roadsides are difficult to interpret, and there are many weeds of roadsides which are considered native in various regions across Britain despite the obvious route of introduction. This uncertainty is nicely summed up by Rumsey,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stewart |first1=A. |title=Scarce Plants in Britain |date=1974 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref> who writes "[it] may be a long-established introduction rather than a native species… and may have been introduced as a seed contaminant of leguminous crops." It is, however, usually treated as native and it is classified as VU (Vulnerable) in the Red List.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |url=https://hub.jncc.gov.uk/assets/cc1e96f8-b105-4dd0-bd87-4a4f60449907}}</ref>

In 2021 [[Natural England]] designated [[Swanscombe Peninsula]] in Kent a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]], partly for its population of yellow vetchling.<ref>{{cite web |title=Notification under Section 28C of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 |url=https://consult.defra.gov.uk/natural-england/swanscombe-peninsula/supporting_documents/1%20%20Swanscombe%20Peninsula%20Notification%20Document%2011%20March%202021.pdf |website=Natural England}}</ref>
